hero.title: Learning that feels like an adventure
hero.lead: Pulsar Kids turns math, geography, history and ecology into games your child will ask to play. No ads, no losing, no scary timers — just the joy of getting it right. And you stay calmly in charge of screen time.
hero.systemLabel: The Solar System: the Sun and the eight planets your child travels through

about.title: Why Pulsar Kids
about.sub: The goal of Pulsar Kids is for children to want to learn — all by themselves. The strongest reason to learn is working something out yourself. So a child reaches every answer with their own head: each task is pitched to be hard enough to think about and still within reach — and the child manages it. Afterwards they can see what they have learned: yesterday they could not add 7 and 8, today they can. That is why they are the ones asking what comes next.

hint.title: A mistake is a hint
hint.text: Nobody loses here. After a mistake a visual hint appears, and the task that didn’t work out comes back once more at the end of the level — to make it stick, not to punish.

voice.title: Play before you can read
voice.text: Tasks and answers are read aloud, and every text has a speaker button next to it. Once your child reads confidently, you can switch the voice off.

steps.title: Difficulty grows with your child
steps.text: Every game is a path of steps, each a little harder than the one before. The stars on a card tell you what age the game is for.

ads.title: No ads
ads.text: No third-party ads. Your child sees only the tasks, their own world and their own achievements.

world.title: A planet of their own that keeps growing
world.sub: Every task earns crystals. What to do with them is your child’s own decision — and that is a little lesson too.

build.title: Build a world
build.text: Crystals can be traded for buildings and decorations for their own planet. The grandest of all — the “dream castle” — unlocks last.

goal.title: Or save up for a family goal
goal.text: You agree on a real-life reward together: “collect 500 crystals and we bake cookies”. Spend now or keep saving — the choice is your child’s.

stations.title: Stations of knowledge
stations.text: Every few steps of any game, a key of knowledge waits for the child. The keys open stations on the planet: an observatory, a library, a laboratory of numbers.

theme.title: A favorite theme
theme.text: Unicorns, space, dinosaurs, the underwater world, bricks, the forest, winter… A theme changes the colors, the hero, the crystals and the city that grows on the planet.

parents.sub: A separate entrance for grown-ups. Your child can’t wander in — the game simply has no door to it.

time.title: Screen time without tears
time.text: You set the session length, the break and the daily limit. Your child sees no timer — just hourglasses that slowly disappear. A level already started is always finished, and then the hero “goes for a rest”.

faq.title: Questions parents ask about Pulsar Kids

what.title: What is Pulsar Kids?
what.text: Pulsar Kids is a set of learning games for kids aged 4–10, played in a browser on a phone, tablet or computer. Across {games} games children practice math, language, logic, geography, history, astronomy, ecology, nature and art, while parents set the screen time.

age.title: What ages is Pulsar Kids for?
age.text: Children from 4 to 10. The games come in three age groups: the stars on a game’s card show what age it suits, and the difficulty grows step by step with the child.

langs.title: Which languages can children play in?
langs.text: English, Ukrainian and Polish. It is not a translated interface: the tasks, hints and voice are written for each language. Parents choose the language of the game and of the voice in the parents’ area.

install.title: Is there an app to install?
install.text: No. Pulsar Kids runs in a modern browser on a phone, tablet or computer — it is not in the app stores. The game page can be added to the device’s home screen.

mistake.title: What happens when a child makes a mistake?
mistake.text: Nobody loses. After two mistakes a visual hint appears, and a missed task comes back once more at the end of the level. There are no “lives” and no red crosses.

time.title: How do parents control screen time?
time.text: In the parents’ area you set the session length, the break and the daily limit. The time is counted on the server, so it is the same on every device the child uses. The child sees no countdown — just hourglasses that slowly disappear — and always finishes a level already started.

ads.title: Are there ads in the game?
ads.text: No, there are no third-party ads. A child sees only the tasks, their own planet and their own achievements.

privacy.title: What data does Pulsar Kids collect about a child?
privacy.text: Only what a parent enters — a name or nickname, a PIN, a year and month of birth — and how the child gets on in the games. There are no ads and no advertising trackers, and a child’s data is never sold or passed to advertisers. Parents can download or delete everything in the parents’ area at any time.

try.title: Can you try it without signing up?
try.text: Yes. The “Try the game now” button opens the first level of the real game with no account and no payment — at the child’s own pace, with no timer. What is collected in a trial game is not saved — for that, a parent creates an account with an email address.

feedback.title: Spotted a bug or have an idea?
feedback.sub: Describe what went wrong, what could be handier or which game is missing. A photo or a short video can be added — it makes things easier to understand.

final.title: Ready for the adventure?
final.sub: The trial game needs no sign-up and no payment.

math.add: The game teaches addition — from 3 + 3 to three-digit numbers. The first steps keep the sums within ten, step twenty already asks 115 + 61, and the last one, the fortieth, sums such as 493 + 42. The child picks the answer out of nine numbers. Every level has ten sums: half of them new, half from earlier steps, so that what was learned stays learned.
math.sub: The game teaches subtraction — from 6 − 5 to three-digit numbers with borrowing. Halfway along the path the sums look like 115 − 89, and on the last step like 493 − 139. The answer is picked out of nine numbers, and every level mixes new sums with familiar ones from earlier steps.
math.mul: The game leads from multiplying by 2 to multiplying two-digit numbers. It begins with 2 × 5 and 2 × 4, step fifteen asks sums such as 6 × 8 and 7 × 10, and the last one, the thirtieth, 14 × 15. The answer is picked out of nine numbers, and what was learned comes back in later levels, so the times tables stay in the head.
math.div: The game teaches sharing equally — from 10 ÷ 2 to sums such as 64 ÷ 8. It starts with dividing by 2, then by 4 and by 5, and so on, step after step — twenty-five in all. The answer is picked out of nine numbers, and familiar sums come back in later levels.
math.mixed: All four operations, mixed up: the child never knows beforehand what the next sum will ask — adding, taking away, multiplying or dividing. Sixty steps lead from 6 − 6 and 2 × 4 to sums such as 1013 − 210. It is mental-math practice for children who already know each operation by itself.
math.fractions: The game introduces fractions through things a child knows well: a pizza, a pie or a chocolate bar is cut into equal pieces, and some of them are colored in. The child names that part — 1/4, 2/3, 3/4 — and picks it out of nine fractions. The game has ten steps.
math.fraction_ops: The next game after “Tasty Fractions”, for children who already know what a fraction is. First come sums with the same denominator (3/5 + 1/5), then with different ones (1/5 + 1/2), and after that subtracting, multiplying and dividing. Twenty steps; the answer is picked from several fractions.
math.geometry: Three skills in one game. First the child builds a picture out of shapes and counts the squares in it. Then comes area — counting the colored squares. At the end of the path the child goes around a shape’s edge to find its perimeter, and looks for the shape with the biggest one. Twenty steps.
math.clock: The game teaches reading a clock with hands. At first the face shows whole hours — 11:00, for example — and the child picks what time it is. Then minutes appear (4:10), and at the end of the path it is the other way round: a time is said in words or written as 17:05, and the child finds the clock that shows it.

logic.shadows: The game trains an eye for shape: a picture has to be recognized by its black outline. At first there are three quite different things, then four and five, and the shadows grow more and more alike — things of one family, later near look-alikes, and with a blurred edge too. Each picture is dragged onto its shadow; a level has five tasks.

language.bubbles: Three games in one, all about Ukrainian letters. First the child pops bubbles with letters in the order they stand in the alphabet. Then words are put together from syllables — “по-мі-дор”, “по-не-ді-лок”. At the end of the path the child hears a word and spells it from letters. Fifty steps, five tasks in every level.
